title: Owingsville: a town named on a wager
summary: In 1795 Colonel Thomas Dye Owings came from Maryland to Kentucky to run iron furnaces, and Owingsville, founded in 1811, took his name after a wager.
bodyMarkdown:
In 1795 Colonel Thomas Dye Owings came to Kentucky from Maryland. His father sent him west to run some of the first iron furnaces in the region. The hills of what became Bath County held iron ore, limestone for flux, and thick forests to burn for charcoal, which is everything an early furnace needed.

Iron was valuable on the frontier. Settlers needed kettles, plows, nails, and tools, and hauling iron over the mountains from the East was slow and costly. Furnaces in this part of northeastern Kentucky helped supply that demand, and the men who ran them could grow rich quickly. Within about fifteen years Owings had built up a good deal of wealth and land.

Owings was not the only big landholder in the area. Colonel Richard H. Menefee also owned a large tract of the ground where a town was taking shape. Both men wanted the new town to carry his name. As the story is told, they settled it with a wager: whoever built the finer house the quickest would win the name.

Owings won. Accounts say the contest cost him a great deal of money, with one telling putting the figure at sixty thousand dollars. The town of Owingsville was founded in 1811, the same year the Kentucky General Assembly formed Bath County from part of Montgomery County. The county took its name from the many mineral springs, or baths, found there. Owingsville became the county seat.

The wager is a local legend, and the details have grown with the telling. The outline is well recorded, though: an ironmaster with money to spend, a rival landowner, and a new county that needed a seat of government.

## Kentucky today

Owingsville is a small city of about 1,600 people near the center of Bath County, where US 60 meets KY 36. It is still the county seat. The map pin marks the town.
